children are more likely to learn in ways similar to those in which they think.
children are born to learn and are equipped with a variety of learning devices.
children's thinking is more powerful than we realize and that schools, even the most successful, are failing in their most important task, teaching for real understanding.

the ways in which people of all ages and backgrounds think, and with the ways in Which schools and other institutions can and should take advantage of these modes of thinking.
the nature of the unschooled mind, and the implications of this unschooled mind for education.
the question, "What is the nature of the knowledge that is most important to learn?"

schools are doing a poor job of teaching for real understanding, that they are doing a better job of teaching for the acquisition of facts and skills, and that this latter accomplishment has a number of positive consequences for society.
schools are failing to help students understand the nature of knowledge, the nature of reality, and the nature of themselves.
the unschooled mind, in spite of its limitations, is the best we have, and it will continue to be so for the foreseeable future.

the mind is a powerful, flexible, self-constructing, and self-correcting system.
we have a long way to go before we are able to teach for understanding, and we have a long, long way to go if we want to teach for understanding in the arts.

the best way to improve the performance of the brain is through the practice of the mind.
